E.2 Enhanced and Advanced Geothermal Next-generation geothermal technologies offer more consistent energy generation and less detectability than other distributed energy resources (DERs), such as solar photovoltaics (PV) and wind. While conventional geothermal (hydrothermal) baseload is available continuously, conventional geothermal systems rely on naturally occurring hydrothermal resources (hot water and steam in porous rock). Enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) can be deployed in a much broader range of geologic settings where high temperatures exist but without the preexisting natural reservoir conditions. EGS use technologies applied to hydraulic fracturing to inject fluid underground to create fractures and improve rock permeability, allowing the fluid to flow within the rock fractures, after which the heated fluid is collected for energy generation (NLR 2025d, DOE EERE 2023). EGS can also include chemicals and additives in addition to physical stimulation to improve permeability (NLR 2025d) to further enhance accessibility to geothermal energy. Closed-loop geothermal (CLG) systems are emerging technologies that are transitioning from pilot-scale demonstrations to early commercial deployments, according to an NLR expert. They represent a novel approach to geothermal energy because they do not rely on fluid exchange with the subsurface. Instead, a sealed loop circulates a working fluid through deep boreholes, absorbing heat from surrounding rock and transferring that heat to the surface for use in power generation or direct heating. One of the challenges associated with this technology is the low heat transfer efficiency. Geothermal heat pumps (GHPs) (also known as ground source heat pumps) are a proven, commercial, and widely available technology used for space heating, cooling, and sometimes water heating. They use the relatively constant temperatures just below the Earth’s surface to provide efficient thermal energy for residential, commercial, and institutional buildings. While CLG systems and GHPs both use a closed-loop circulation of fluid, they serve different purposes. CLG systems circulate fluid through deep, hot rock formations for electricity generation or direct heating. GHPs use shallow ground temperatures near the surface for space heating and cooling in buildings (NLR 2025a). CLGs and GHPs can increase energy efficiency and cut costs but are primarily suitable for smaller scale (i.e., building-level) applications (DOE 2023a). CLGs and GHPs make geothermal a possible option in more areas than when relying on natural geothermal features, yet they do not require the reservoir stimulation needed with EGS, reducing costs and water demand (NLR 2025a); however, according to an interviewee, this approach may require higher temperatures compared to EGS, limiting applicability to areas with specific natural geologic characteristics.
